props.title: Immortel (ad vitam)

sections.content: Immortel (ad vitam) represents a fascinating experiment in early digital-practical hybrid filmmaking, following in the footsteps of Sky Captain and the World of Tomorrow (2004). Based on Enki Bilal's comic series, the film merges live actors with CGI characters in a dystopian 2095 New York, creating a unique aesthetic that bridges European comic art and cyberpunk cinema. Like The Fifth Element (1997), it embraces a distinctly French approach to sci-fi worldbuilding, though with darker undertones.

sections.content: The film's integration of Egyptian mythology into futuristic storytelling creates an unusual narrative thread that later influenced works like Gods of Egypt (2016) and Moon Knight (2022). Director Bilal's background as a comic artist shows in every frame, with compositions that feel lifted directly from graphic novel panels. This approach to visual storytelling shares DNA with Sin City (2005), though Immortel's execution leans more experimental.

The film's troubled production and mixed reception highlight the challenges of early 2000s CGI-heavy filmmaking. While some effects haven't aged well, the ambitious vision anticipates later successful mergers of live-action and digital elements like 300 (2006) and Speed Racer (2008). The film's striking blue-tinted cinematography and industrial design aesthetic influenced later sci-fi works like Priest (2011) and Dredd (2012). SUBHEAD: European Science Fiction Cinema Evolution

sections.content: Immortel represents a crucial bridge between European comic-inspired science fiction and modern digital filmmaking. Its DNA can be traced through later works like Valerian and the City of a Thousand Planets (2017), which similarly adapted famous French comics with heavy CGI elements. The film's ambitious but flawed execution paved the way for more successful European sci-fi ventures like District 13 (2004) and Ares (2016).
